[∇×(a×b)]i​​=ϵijk​∂j​(ϵklm​al​bm​)=(δil​δjm​−δim​δjl​)∂j​(al​bm​)=∂j​(ai​bj​−aj​bi​)=ai​∂j​bj​−bi​∂j​aj​+bj​∂j​ai​−aj​∂j​bi​.​
(1)
The last equality is the product rule. Recognizing the divergences and directional derivatives proves the curl of a cross product identity:
∇×(a×b)=a(∇⋅b)−b(∇⋅a)+(b⋅∇)a−(a⋅∇)b.​

The divergence theorem states that, for a continuously differentiable vector field H on a bounded region V with piecewise smooth boundary S and outward unit normal n^,
∫V​∇⋅HdV=∫S​H⋅n^dS.
(3)
To apply it, first derive the divergence of a cross product using the Levi-Civita symbol and the product rule:
∇⋅(F×G)​=ϵijk​∂i​(Fj​Gk​)=ϵijk​(∂i​Fj​)Gk​+ϵijk​Fj​∂i​Gk​=G⋅(∇×F)−F⋅(∇×G).​
(4)
In the second term the minus sign comes from interchanging the first two indices of the Levi-Civita symbol. The divergence theorem with H=F×G now yields
∫V​[G⋅(∇×F)−F⋅(∇×G)]dV=∫S​(F×G)⋅n^dS.​
(5)

For separation of variables, take n=T(t)X(x)Y(y)Z(z) and divide the reaction-diffusion equation by this product wherever it is nonzero:
μTT′​−μγ​=XX′′​+YY′′​+ZZ′′​.
(8)
Each spatial term depends on a different variable and must be constant. Write X′′=−kx2​X and similarly for the other two factors. The Dirichlet boundary conditions give X(0)=X(L)=0. A zero separation constant permits only a linear function and hence the zero solution; a positive value of X′′/X likewise permits no nonzero function vanishing at both endpoints. The nontrivial choices are therefore
Xp​(x)=sinLpπx​,Yq​(y)=sinLqπy​,Zr​(z)=sinLrπz​,p,q,r=1,2,….​
(9)
The temporal ordinary differential equation is
Tp,q,r′​=[γ−L2μπ2​(p2+q2+r2)]Tp,q,r​,
(10)
so, absorbing its constant multiplier into ap,q,r​,
Tp,q,r​(t)=exp{[γ−L2μπ2​(p2+q2+r2)]t}.​
(11)
The superposition principle and completeness of the Fourier sine series give the stated threefold expansion with these factors. For an initial density n0​, orthogonality also determines the constants:
ap,q,r​=L38​∫0L​∫0L​∫0L​n0​(x,y,z)sinLpπx​sinLqπy​sinLrπz​dxdydz.
(12)

Solution

Words: 102
b OurBigBook.com
The fastest temporal growth occurs for the lowest spatial eigenvalue, with p=q=r=1. Its growth rate is
s111​=γ−L23μπ2​.
(13)
For a generic initial condition its coefficient is nonzero, so this term determines the long-time behavior. In fact, every nonzero, nonnegative initial density has a111​>0, since the product of the three first sine eigenfunctions is strictly positive in the interior. Consequently
Lcrit​=πγ3μ​​,exponential growth precisely when L>Lcrit​.​
(14)
For L<Lcrit​ every term decays. At equality the first term is stationary and all higher terms decay: equality does not produce exponential growth. This is a reaction-diffusion equation threshold arising from competition between production and loss through the Dirichlet boundary condition.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
The separation of variables solution with Dirichlet boundary conditions on the cuboid is
n=p,q,r≥1∑​ap,q,r​sinλLpπx​sinLqπλ​y​sinLrπλ​z​exp{[γ−L2μπ2​(λ2p2​+λq2+λr2)]t}.​
(15)
The constants are fixed by the initial density through Fourier sine series. The fastest term again has p=q=r=1. When L=2Lcrit​, its growth rate becomes
s111​=γ[1−121​(λ−2+2λ)].
(16)
Thus the precise condition for no exponentially growing term is
λ−2+2λ≥12,equivalently 2λ3−12λ2+1≥0,λ>0.​
(17)
For example, λ=1/4 gives λ−2+2λ=33/2>12, while λ=6 gives 12+1/36>12: either a sufficiently flat or a sufficiently elongated cuboid suppresses growth despite its unchanged volume. The function λ−2+2λ decreases to its minimum 3 at λ=1, then increases without bound. Hence there are two positive threshold values, with growth only between them; equality leaves one stationary term and all other terms decaying.

(xn+1u′)′=0.

uh​(x)=A+Bx−n(n=0),uh​(x)=A+Blogx(n=0).​

Choose the convention Lx​G(x,s)=δ(x−s), where δ is the Dirac delta distribution, together with G(1/2,s)=G(1,s)=0. The Green's function is continuous at x=s and obeys
∂x​G(s+,s)−∂x​G(s−,s)=1.
(20)
These conditions follow by integrating its differential equation across s; continuity prevents a derivative of the Dirac delta distribution. If ℓ and r are homogeneous solutions satisfying the left and right boundary conditions, respectively, and W=ℓr′−ℓ′r is their Wronskian, then
G(x,s)=W(s)ℓ(x<​)r(x>​)​,x<​=min(x,s),x>​=max(x,s).
(21)
For n=0 take ℓ(x)=x−n−2n and r(x)=x−n−1. Their Wronskian is W(s)=n(2n−1)s−n−1, and hence
Gn​(x,s)=n(2n−1)sn+1(x<−n​−2n)(x>−n​−1)​,n=0.​
(22)
For n=0 take ℓ(x)=log(2x) and r(x)=logx, giving W(s)=log2/s and
G0​(x,s)=log2s​log(2x<​)logx>​.​
(23)
Both formulas satisfy the endpoint conditions, continuity, and the unit jump directly. The unique solution of the boundary value problem is
u(x)=∫1/21​Gn​(x,s)f(s)ds.​
(24)
The factor sn+1 in the first formula matters: this Green's function is for the original monic differential operator, with ordinary measure ds, rather than for the operator multiplied by xn+1.

u(x)=n(2n−1)r(x)∫1/2x​(1−2nsn)ds+ℓ(x)∫x1​(1−sn)ds​.

For n=−1, the two integrals are
I1​=x−21​−n+12n​(xn+1−2−n−1),I2​=1−x−n+11−xn+1​.

Substitution and simplification yield
u(x)=n+11​[x−1+2(2n−1)x−n−1​],n=0,−1.​

At x=1 both contributions vanish. At x=1/2 the bracket is −1/2+(2n−1)/[2(2n−1)]=0. The differential operator kills x−n−1 and sends x/(n+1) to 1/x, so this also verifies the inhomogeneous equation.

and the Green's function integral becomes

Here L=d2/dx2, and u′′=1/x. Explicitly u(1)=0 and u(1/2)=−(log2)/2+(log2)/2=0. Thus both exceptional and nonexceptional formulas satisfy the required boundary conditions.

h(k)​=∫R​∫R​e−ikxf(x−x′)g(x′)dx′dx=∫R​∫R​e−ik(y+x′)f(y)g(x′)dydx′=(∫R​e−ikyf(y)dy)(∫R​e−ikx′g(x′)dx′).​

h(k)=f​(k)g​(k).​

U=6​1​​3​11+i​−i3​i−1+i​0−21+i​​.​

For the unitary matrix C, C−1=C†. Therefore D=C−1AC is a Hermitian matrix:
D†=(C†AC)†=C†AC=D.
(44)
Every positive integer power remains a Hermitian matrix, since (Dp)†=(D†)p=Dp. Its eigenvalues are real by the finite-dimensional spectral theorem. Equivalently, matrix similarity gives
Dp=C−1ApC,

whose eigenvalues are λjp​∈R​, where the λj​ are the real eigenvalues of A.

vi OurBigBook.com
Complete the square in the Hermitian matrix polynomial:
H=(A+2α​I)2+(β−4α2​)I.
(46)
For every nonzero vector v,
v†Hv=​(A+2α​I)v​2+(β−4α2​)∥v∥2>0.
(47)
Thus H is a positive-definite matrix, so 0 is not an eigenvalue of H​. In finite-dimensional spectral theorem terms, each eigenvalue is
hj​=λj2​+αλj​+β=(λj​+2α​)2+β−4α2​>0.
(48)
If α2≥4β, the scalar polynomial has real roots of a polynomial
r±​=2−α±α2−4β​​.
(49)
An allowed nonzero root can be an eigenvalue of A, a Hermitian matrix which is also an invertible matrix, in which case H has a zero eigenvalue. For example, α=2, β=1, A=−I gives H=0. The weaker inequality does not force failure for every A; it removes the general positive lower bound. There is also the harmless corner α=β=0, for which H=A2 stays positive definite because A is invertible, even though the strict discriminant hypothesis is absent.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
For a holomorphic function, the derivative supplied by complex differentiability must have the same value along real and imaginary increments. Those two computations give
f′(z)=ux​+ivx​=iuy​+ivy​​=vy​−iuy​.
(62)
Equating real and imaginary parts proves the Cauchy-Riemann equations:
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​.​
(63)
Conversely, if the first partial derivatives are continuous near a point and obey these equations there, real differentiability gives
f(z+h)−f(z)=(ux​+ivx​)Reh+(uy​+ivy​)Imh+o(∣h∣)=f′(z)h+o(∣h∣),
(64)
which proves complex differentiability under this regularity assumption.
The gradients of the real and imaginary parts have dot product
∇u⋅∇v=ux​vx​+uy​vy​=vy​vx​−vx​vy​=0,
(65)
and ∣∇u∣2=∣∇v∣2=∣f′(z)∣2. At every point with f′(z)=0, the two level sets are regular curves, their gradients are nonzero normal vectors, and their tangent directions are therefore perpendicular.
The printed phrase "at every point" needs this regular-point qualification. At a critical point with f′(z)=0, the level sets may cross or fail to have a unique tangent. For example, f(z)=z2 gives u=x2−y2 and v=2xy: at the origin the zero level sets are respectively the diagonals and the coordinate axes. Thus the valid conclusion is orthogonality at every regular intersection, where f′(z)=0​.

sin2zz2​=(z−z3/6+O(z5)z​)2=1+3z2​+O(z4),
(72)
so z=0 is removable, with extended value 1​. Every other z=nπ is a double pole, since the numerator is nonzero there. There are no finite zeros, including after removal at zero.
At infinity the double poles nπ accumulate. Equivalently, after z=1/w, the function 1/[w2sin2(1/w)] has double poles at w=1/(nπ) tending to zero. Hence ∞ is a non-isolated singularity​. The removable/pole/essential trichotomy for isolated singularities does not apply there; calling this an isolated essential singularity would be incorrect.

The generalized momentum of this Lagrangian is
p=∂x˙∂L​=1−x˙2​mx˙​,∂x∂L​=−V′(x).
(89)
The Euler-Lagrange equation therefore gives
dtd​(1−x˙2​mx˙​)+V′(x)=0,(1−x˙2)3/2mx¨​=−V′(x).​
(90)
Because L has no explicit time dependence, the energy form of the Beltrami identity gives a conserved quantity E=x˙∂L/∂x˙−L. Here
E=1−x˙2​mx˙2​+m1−x˙2​+V(x)=1−x˙2​m​+V(x)​.
(91)
For a direct check of conservation of energy, differentiate:
dtdE​=x˙[(1−x˙2)3/2mx¨​+V′(x)]=0.
(92)
This is the rest-plus-kinetic energy of a relativistic particle, in units with light speed one, plus its potential energy.

Write ΔV=V2​−V1​>0 and γi​=(1−vi2​)−1/2, the initial Lorentz factor. The conserved energy from part (a) is E=mγi​+V1​. To emerge on the higher plateau with positive speed, the particle needs E>m+V2​. Hence
γi​>1+mΔV​,vi​>vth​=1−(1+mΔV​)−2​.​
(93)
Above this threshold, conservation of energy gives γf​=γi​−ΔV/m>1. The transmitted velocity is positive, so
vf​=+1−[1−vi2​​1​−mΔV​]−2​,vi​>vth​.​
(94)
Below threshold there is a turning point within the steep transition, where x˙=0 and V=E−m<V2​. The particle returns to the lower plateau. Its final potential energy equals its initial value, so its final Lorentz factor equals γi​ but its direction is reversed:
vf​=−vi​,0<vi​<vth​.​
(95)
At exact threshold the limiting speed on the upper plateau is zero. This is the marginal case, not passage with positive outgoing speed. The ideal discontinuous potential does not specify the detailed trajectory at equality; a smooth transition can make the particle approach the top asymptotically. The final-speed formulas above cover the strictly transmitted and reflected regimes requested.

Take nonzero real trial functions y with y,y′ square-integrable and sufficient decay for integration by parts. For a compactly supported variation y↦y+εη, the first variations are
δF=2∫R​(y′η′−V0​e−x2yη)dx=2∫R​(−y′′−V0​e−x2y)ηdx,δG=2∫R​yηdx.
(96)
The quotient rule for the functional then yields
δΛ=G[y]2​∫R​[−y′′−V0​e−x2y−Λ[y]y]ηdx.
(97)
By the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations, stationarity for all such η is equivalent to
−y′′−V0​e−x2y=Λ[y]y.
(98)
Conversely, multiplying a decaying eigenfunction equation by y and using integration by parts gives F[y]=EG[y], so its Rayleigh quotient equals E and its first variation vanishes. Thus the stationary values of the functional are the energy eigenvalues. The word "extrema" in the question includes stationary points here: higher eigenfunctions can be saddle points of the unrestricted Rayleigh quotient.
The Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle gives
E0​=y=0inf​Λ[y],E0​≤Λ[yT​].​
(99)
Choose an admissible trial family, calculate its Rayleigh quotient, and minimize over its parameters to obtain the best upper bound within that family. Equality holds for the exact ground state; a restricted family generally gives only an upper bound.

For the trial function, yT′​=−axyT​. The required Gaussian integrals are
G[yT​]=∫R​e−ax2dx=aπ​​,∫R​x2e−ax2dx=2a3/2π​​.
(100)
The second formula follows by differentiating the first with respect to a. Therefore
F[yT​]=a22a3/2π​​−V0​1+aπ​​,
(101)
and division by G[yT​] gives the Gaussian variational bound for an attractive Gaussian well:
E(a)=2a​−V0​1+aa​​,a>0.​
(102)
This is a good trial family because it consists of smooth, positive, square-integrable functions decaying at both infinities. Each is an even function, matching the symmetry of the lowest bound state in this even potential, and the parameter varies its width. It also permits exact Gaussian integrals. Its Gaussian tail need not equal the exact exponential tail of a negative-energy bound state for the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle to give a valid bound.
